¶
'''undeify''' (un-dē′i-fī), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''undeified'', ppr. ''undeifying''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''deify''.] To reduce from the state of deity; deprive of the character or qualities of a god; deprive of the honor due to a god. ''Addison'', Spectator, No. 73.

'''undelectable''' (un-dẹ̄-lek′ta-bl), ''a.'' Not delectable or pleasant. ''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, iii. 209.

'''undelegated''' (un-del′ẹ̄-gā-ted), ''a.'' Not delegated; not deputed; not granted.
{{smaller block|Your assumption of ''undelegated'' power.
{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}}}

'''undeliberate''' (un-dẹ̄-lib′e̤-rāt), ''a.'' Not deliberate. ''Lowell'', Agassiz, iii. 1.

'''undelighted''' (un-dẹ̄-lī′ted), ''a.'' Not delighted; not well pleased.
{{smaller block|<poem>The fiend
Saw, ''undelighted'', all delight.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 286.}}}}

'''undelightful''' (un-dẹ̄-līt′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not giving delight or great pleasure.

'''undemocratize''' (un-dẹ̄-mok′ra-tīz), ''v. t.'' To render undemocratic. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Its consequence was to ''undemocratize'' the Democratic party, and secure its final defeat.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXIII. 255.}}}}

'''undemonstrable''' (un-dẹ̄-mon′stra-bl), ''a.'' Indemonstrable. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. § 9.

'''undemonstrative''' (un-dẹ̄-mon′strā-tiv), ''a.'' Not demonstrative or given to excited or strong expression of feeling; reserved, from modesty, diffidence, or policy: as, an ''undemonstrative'' person; ''undemonstrative'' manners.

'''undependable''' (un-dẹ̄-pen′da̤-bl), ''a.'' Not dependable.

'''undepending†''' (un-dẹ̄-pen′ding), ''a.'' Not dependent; independent.

'''undepraved''' (un-dẹ̄-prāvd′), ''a.'' Not depraved or corrupted. ''V. Knox'', Essays, No. 70.

'''undepreciated''' (un-dẹ̄-prē′shi-ā-ted), ''a.'' Not depreciated or lowered in value: as, ''undepreciated'' bank-notes.

'''undepressed''' (un-dẹ̄-prest′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not pressed down; not lowered; not sunk below the surface.

'''2.''' Not depressed, dejected, or cast down.

[< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''deify''.] To reduce from the state of deity; deprive of the character or qualities of a god; deprive of the honor due to a god. ''Addison'', Spectator, No. 73.

'''undelectable''' (un-dẹ̄-lek′ta-bl), ''a.'' Not delectable or pleasant. ''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, iii. 209.

{{smaller block|Your assumption of ''undelegated'' power.
{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}}}

'''undelighted''' (un-dẹ̄-lī′ted), ''a.'' Not delighted; not well pleased.

'''undemonstrable''' (un-dẹ̄-mon′stra-bl), ''a.'' Indemonstrable. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. § 9.

'''undemonstrative''' (un-dẹ̄-mon′strā-tiv), ''a.'' Not demonstrative or given to excited or strong expression of feeling; reserved, from modesty, diffidence, or policy: as, an ''undemonstrative'' person; ''undemonstrative'' manners.

'''undeniable''' (un-dẹ̄-nī′a-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Incapable of being denied; indisputable; evidently true; of being denied, indisputable, evidently true: as, ''undeniable'' evidence; his ability is ''undeniable''.—'''2.''' Decidedly and unmistakably good; excellent. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|The daylight, furnished gratis, was certainly “''undeniable''” in its quality.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Roman Meals.}}
Wise dissenting matrons were divided between fear lest their sons should want to marry her, and resentment that she should treat those ''undeniable'' young men with a distant scorn.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, vi.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' Indubitable, incontrovertible, unquestionable, incontestable.}}

'''undeniableness''' (un-dē-nī′a-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being undeniable. ''Nineteenth Century'', XXII. 404.

'''undeniably''' (un-dẹ̄-nī′a-bli), ''adv.'' So plainly as to admit of no contradiction or denial; indisputably. ''Locke'', Human Understanding, iv. 11.

'''undenominational''' (un-dē-nom-i-nā′shọn-al), ''a.'' Not denominational; not pertaining to a denomination; not professing the tenets of a denomination; not in the interests of or confined to any denomination; unsectarian: as, an ''undenominational'' charity or society.

'''undenominationalism''' (un-dē-nom-i-nā′shọn-al-izm), ''n.'' The absence of denominationalism, or of denominational teaching.

{{smaller block|The Education Act of 1870 practically establishes a new religion, ''undenominationalism'', for the elementary schools of the country.
{{right|''Contemporary Rev.'', LIV. 645.}}}}

'''undepartable†''' (un-dē-pär′ta̤-bl), ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''departable''.] That cannot be parted from; inseparable.

{{smaller block|No wys man ne may dowte of ''undepartable'' peyne of the shrewes.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boethius, iv. prose 3.}}}}

'''undependable''' (un-dẹ̄-pen′da̤-bl), ''a.'' Not dependable.

'''undepending†''' (un-dẹ̄-pen′ding), ''a.'' Not dependent; independent.
{{smaller block|We may confidently conclude it never will be otherwise while they are thus upheld ''undepending'' on the Church, on which alone they anciently depended.
{{right|''Milton'', Touching Hirelings.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>One hillock, ye may note, is small and low,
Sunk almost to the level of the plain
By weight of time: the others, ''undepressed.''</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion, vi.}}}}
'''2.''' Not depressed, dejected, or cast down.
{{smaller block|Disarmed but ''undepressed.'' ''Byron'', The Corsair, st. 8.}}

'''undeprived''' (un-dẹ̄-prīvd′), ''a.'' Not deprived, stripped, or dispossessed of any property, right, or the like; not divested by authority. ''Dryden'', Character of a Good Parson.

'''under''' (un′dėr), ''prep.'' and ''adv.'' [< ME. ''under'', ''undur'', ''undir'', ''undyr'', ''onder'', < AS. ''under'' = OS. ''undar'' = OFries. ''under'', ''onder'' = D. ''onder'' = MLG. ''under'', LG. ''under'', ''unner'' = OHG. ''untar'', under'', MHG. G. ''unter'', under, among, = Icel. ''undir'' = Sw. Dan. ''under'' = Goth. ''undar'', under; perhaps akin to L. ''infra'', below, ''inferus'', lower (see ''infra-'', ''inferior''), = Skt. ''adhara'', lower, ''adhas'', below; less prob. connected to L. ''inter'', between, among, = Oscan ''anter'', under, within.] '''I.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' Below; beneath: expressing position with reference to that which is above, whether in immediate contact or not, or which towers aloft, surmounts, covers, or overtops: as, all ''under'' heaven; ''under'' the earth or the sea; ''under'' the surface; ''under'' the table; to take shelter ''under'' a tree; to live ''under'' the same roof; to hide a thing ''under'' a heap of straw; to hide one’s light ''under'' a bushel; to overhear a conversation ''under'' one’s windows.
{{smaller block|<poem>It happed hym to ride
In al this care ''under'' a forest side.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 134.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Under'' the churche of the sayd Syon is the sepulture or beryall of prophete and kynge of Israell.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 20.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Under'' these palaces was the private enclosed port of the Kings, . . . where the Turks, till within this fifty years, obliged all foreign ships to ride, not suffering them to anchor ''under'' the castle, as they do at present.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, I. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|They clambered the ascent to the castle in silence, and arrived ''under'' the dark shadow of its towers without being discovered.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 30.}}}}
{{smaller block|The citizens beheld with anxiety the encampment of this formidable force ''under'' their walls.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Whereon a hundred stately beeches grew,
And here and there great hollies ''under'' them.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Pelleas and Ettarre.}}}}

'''2.''' In or at a place, point, or position that is lower than; further down than; immediately below: as, to hit a man ''under'' the belt; to have pains ''under'' the arms.
{{smaller block|The spear smote him ''under'' the fifth rib. {{right|2 Sam. ii. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He most happily
Shot him ''under'' his collar-bone.</poem>
{{right|''Sir Andrew Barton'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 207).}}}}

'''3.''' In the position or state of, or while bearing, supporting, sustaining, receiving, suffering, undergoing, or the like: as, to sink ''under'' a load; to act ''under'' great excitement.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fainting ''under''
The pleasing punishment.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., i. 1. 46.}}}}
{{smaller block|The remedy which you alledge is the very disease we groan ''under''. {{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, i. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|My Lord Sommers thought of me last year for the Bishoprick of Waterford; so my Lord President may now think on me for that of Cork, if the incumbent dyes of the spotted feaver he is now ''under''.
{{right|''Swift'', in Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 343.}}}}
{{smaller block|Next, when he was trembling in prayer ''under'' a fear that no word of God could help him, this part of a sentence darted in upon him, “My grace is sufficient.”
{{right|''Southey'', Life of Bunyan, p. 31.}}}}

'''4.''' Inferior to in point of rank, dignity, social position, or the like.
{{smaller block|It was too great an honour for any man ''under'' a duke.
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}
{{smaller block|No person ''under'' a diviner can with any prospect of veracity conduct a correspondence at such an arm’s length.
{{right|''Lamb'', Distant Correspondents.}}}} '''5.''' Inferior to or less than, with respect to number, amount, quantity, value, age, etc.; falling short of; in or to a less degree than; hence, at, for, or with less than: as, it cannot be bought ''under'' $20.
{{smaller block|Gold and silver, whereof money is made, they do so use as none of them doth more esteem it than the very nature of the thing deserved. And then, who doth not plainly see how far it is ''under'' iron? as without the which men can no better live than without fire and water.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|Three sones he dying left, all ''under'' age.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. x. 64.}}}}
{{smaller block|Medicines take effect sometimes ''under'' and sometimes above the natural proportion of their virtue.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity.}}}}
{{smaller block|There are several hundred parishes in England ''under'' twenty pounds a year.
{{right|''Swift.''}}}}
'''6.''' Of sounds, inferior to, in pitch.—'''7.''' Subject to. {{smaller|(''a'') In a position of submission or subordination to.}}
{{smaller block|At this court in the third month Passaconaway, the chief sachem of Merimack, and his sons came and submitted themselves and their people and lands ''under'' our jurisdiction.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, II. 263.}}}}
{{smaller block|One who by his own act places himself ''under'' authority cannot make conditions about his submission.
{{right|''Pusey'', Eirenicon, p. 197.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Liable or exposed to: as, ''under'' fire; ''under'' the penalty of fine or imprisonment.}}
{{smaller block|''Under'' pain of greater displeasure, we must rest contented.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Subject to the government, rule, command, direction, orders, guidance, or instruction of: as, to serve ''under'' Wellington; I studied ''under'' him; to sit ''under'' a favorite preacher.}}
{{smaller block|And als moche takethe the Amyralle be him allone as alle the other Souldyours han ''undre'' hym.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 38.}}
Happy are they, and onely they, that are ''vnder'' this glorious and gracious Souereigntie: insomuch that I accompt all those abiects that be not hir subiects.
{{right|''Lyly'', Euphues and his England, p. 454.}}
''Under'' which king, Bezonian? Speak or die!
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., v. 3. 118.}}
According to the usual custom, the great caravan, ''under'' the conduct of the governor of Jerusalem, set out for the river Jordan on Easter Monday.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. 30.}}
''Under'' him were many good and sound scholars bred.
{{right|''Lamb'', Christ’s Hospital.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') Subject to the influence or operation of; actuated by.}}
{{smaller block|The Priests and Levites, a Tribe, were of a far different Constitution from this of our Ministers ''under'' the Gospel.
{{right|''Milton'', Touching Hirelings.}}
I shall, in the first place, take care of one who is ''under'' the most subtle species of pride that I have observed in my whole experience. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 127.}}}}
'''8.''' In accordance with; in conformity with: as, to sell out ''under'' the rule.
{{smaller block|He speakes ''vnder'' rule and prescription, and dare not shew his teeth without Machiauell.
''Bp. Earle'', Micro-cosmographie, A too idly reseru’d Man.
We have . . . spent some time in hearing both parties, concerning the bounds of those patents ''under'' which yourselves and the other governments do claim.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, II. 387.}}
The commentators and lawyers have agreed that, ''under'' these circumstances, the marriage must be dissolved.
{{right|''E. W. Lane'', Modern Egyptians, I. 121.}}}}
'''9.''' Bound by: as, to be ''under'' bonds, or a vow.

{{smaller block|The greater part of mankind is slow of apprehension; and therefore, in many cases, ''under'' a necessity of seeing with other men’s eyes. {{right|''South'', Sermons.}}}}
'''10.''' In: with reference to circumstances.
{{smaller block|<poem>To those that live
''Under'' thy care, good rules and patterns give.</poem>
{{right|''Denham'', Of Prudence.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I maun be bound to a foreign land,
And now I’m ''under'' hiding.</poem>
{{right|''Sir James the Rose'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 74).}}}}
{{smaller block|I found the knight ''under'' his butler’s hands, who always shaves him. {{right|''Addison'', Sir Roger in Westminster Abbey.}}}}
'''11.''' In: with reference to category, division, section, class, etc.: as, to treat several topics ''under'' one head.
{{smaller block|''Under'' the double capacity of a poet and a divine. {{right|''Felton'', On the Classicks.}}}}
{{smaller block|The lower blunt-headed summit which we had learned to detest ''under'' the name of Mount Avron. {{right|''Forbes'', Ex. of War, II. 176.}}}}
'''12.''' In course of: as, to be ''under'' treatment, or ''under'' discussion.—'''13.''' In the form or style of; by the appearance or show of; with the character, designation, pretense, pretext, or cover of.
{{smaller block|But I do aduertyse you to lyne your Iacket ''vnder'' this fasshyon or maner. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 247.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He thoght his falshed to feyne, ''vndur'' faire wordes,
And his cautels to colour vnder coynt speche.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 11490.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is one of his most crafty and subtle assaults to send his warriors forth ''under'' the badge of God. {{right|''Latimer'', Misc. Selections.}}}}
{{smaller block|We read that Kinges & Princes haue written great volumes and publisht them ''vnder'' their owne regall titles. {{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 16.}}}}

{{smaller block|Whosoeuer ''vnder'' one name or poesie payeth three pound in ready money shall receiue six shillings and eight pence.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' True Travels, II. 25.}}
Art is here represented ''under'' the person of Vulcan.
{{right|''Bacon'', Physical Fables, v., Expl.}}}}
'''14.''' During the time or existence of: said especially of rulers and their period of rule: as, Christ suffered ''under'' Pontius Pilate; the Armada was destroyed ''under'' the reign of Elizabeth; the American revolution broke out ''under'' the administration of Lord North.
{{smaller block|The remainder of the demesne was sold ''under'' the commonwealth.
{{right|''S. Dowell'', Taxes in England, II. 28.}}}}
'''15.''' With the sanction, authorization, permission, or protection of: as, ''under'' favor; ''under'' leave; ''under'' protection, etc.
{{smaller block|''Under'' whose countenance we steal.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 2. 33.}}
''Under'' favour, there are other materials for a commonwealth besides stark love and kindness.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier.''}}}}
{{smaller block|[The preposition ''under'' in adverbial phrases often coalesces with its noun to form an adverb, from which the adjective or noun may be derived: as, ''under ground'', > ''underground'', ''adv.'', > ''underground'', ''a.''; ''under hand'', > ''underhand'', ''adv.'', > ''underhand'', ''a.''; so ''underboard'', ''underearth'', ''underfoot'', etc. Such forms are not true compounds, but are coalesced phrases, like ''aground'', ''aboard'', ''afoot'', etc.]}}
'''Note under hand†.''' {{smaller|See ''note''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''Under a cloud.''' {{smaller|See ''cloud''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''Under arms,''' {{smaller|armed and equipped for military or naval service.}}—'''Under bare poles.''' {{smaller|See ''bare''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''Under cloud†, conviction, correction,''' {{smaller|etc. See the nouns.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
